content: 1. If erythromycin is necessary, the initial dose of colchicine may need to be reduced, and the maximum dose of colchicine should also be lowered. 2. Patients should be closely monitored for clinical signs of colchicine toxicity. 3. Pregnancy: FDA Pregnancy Category B: Studies in female rats fed erythromycin base (up to 0.25% of their diet) before and during mating, gestation, and through weaning of two successive litters showed no evidence of teratogenicity or adverse effects on reproduction. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Since animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, erythromycin should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) Pregnancy Category: There is no specific guidance from ADEC regarding the use of erythromycin in pregnant women. 4. Labor and Delivery: The effects of erythromycin on labor and delivery are unknown. 5. Nursing Mothers: Erythromycin is excreted in human breast milk. Caution should be exercised when administering erythromycin to nursing women. 6. Pediatric Use: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in pediatric patients. 7. Geriatric Use: Clinical studies with erythromycin delayed-release capsules did not include enough subjects aged 65 and older to determine if they respond differently from younger patients. Other clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. Dose selection for elderly patients should be cautious, typically starting at the lower end of the dosing range, reflecting the higher likelihood of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, and the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. Elderly patients may be more susceptible to developing torsades de pointes arrhythmias compared to younger patients. Elderly patients may experience increased effects of oral anticoagulant therapy while being treated with erythromycin. Erythromycin delayed-release capsules (250 mg) do not contain sodium or potassium. 8. Gender: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in specific gender populations. 9. Race: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in specific racial populations. 10. Renal Impairment: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in patients with renal impairment. 11. Hepatic Impairment: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in patients with hepatic impairment. 12. Females of Reproductive Potential and Males: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in women of reproductive potential and men. 13. Immunocompromised Patients: There is no FDA guidance on the use of erythromycin in immunocompromised patients. 14. Administration and Monitoring: Administration: Erythromycin is administered orally. Monitoring: Limited information is available regarding the monitoring of erythromycin in the drug label. 15. IV Compatibility: Limited information is available regarding the IV compatibility of erythromycin in the drug label. 16. Overdosage: Acute Overdose: In the event of an overdose, erythromycin should be discontinued. Erythromycin is not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis. Chronic Overdose: Limited information is available regarding chronic overdose of erythromycin in the drug label. 17. Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action: Erythromycin inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunits of susceptible organisms. It does not affect nucleic acid synthesis. Structure: Erythromycin delayed-release capsules contain enteric-coated pellets of erythromycin base for oral administration. Each capsule contains 250 mg of erythromycin base. Inactive ingredients include cellulosic polymers, citrate ester, D&C Red No. 30, D&C Yellow No. 10, magnesium stearate, and povidone. The capsule shell contains FD&C Blue No. 1, FD&C Red No. 3, gelatin, and titanium dioxide. Erythromycin is produced by a strain of Saccharopolyspora erythraea (formerly Streptomyces erythraeus) and belongs to the macrolide group of antibiotics. It is basic and readily forms salts with acids, but the base is microbiologically active. 18. Pharmacokinetics: Orally administered erythromycin base and its salts are readily absorbed in the microbiologically active form. Interindividual variations in absorption are observed, and some patients do not achieve acceptable serum levels. Erythromycin is largely bound to plasma proteins, with the freely dissociating bound fraction representing 90% of the total erythromycin absorbed. After absorption, erythromycin diffuses readily into most body fluids. In the absence of meningeal inflammation, low concentrations are normally achieved in the spinal fluid, but the drug's passage across the blood-brain barrier increases in meningitis. The drug is excreted in human milk and crosses the placental barrier, but fetal plasma levels are low. Erythromycin is not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis. In the presence of normal hepatic function, erythromycin is concentrated in the liver and excreted in the bile. The effect of hepatic dysfunction on biliary excretion of erythromycin is not known. After oral administration, less than 5% of the administered dose can be recovered in the active form in the urine. The enteric coating of pellets in erythromycin delayed-release capsules protects the erythromycin base from inactivation by gastric acidity. Due to their small size and enteric coating, the pellets pass intact from the stomach to the small intestine and dissolve efficiently, allowing uniform absorption of erythromycin. After administration of a single dose of a 250 mg erythromycin delayed-release capsule, peak serum levels in the range of 1.13 to 1.68 mcg/mL are attained in approximately 3 hours and decline to 0.30 to 0.42 mcg/mL in 6 hours. Optimal conditions for stability in the presence of gastric secretion and for complete absorption are achieved when erythromycin is taken on an empty stomach. 19. Mechanism of Resistance: The major route of resistance is modification of the 23S rRNA in the 50S ribosomal subunit to insensitivity, while efflux can also be significant. 20. Interaction with Other Antimicrobials: Antagonism exists in vitro between erythromycin and clindamycin, lincomycin, and chloramphenicol. 21. Spectrum of Activity: Erythromycin has been shown to be active against most isolates of the following bacteria both in vitro and in clinical infections: Gram-positive bacteria: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Corynebacterium minutissimum, Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes. Gram-negative bacteria: Bordetella pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Other microorganisms: Chlamydia trachomatis.
